questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a torque measures about a chosen pivot
questions.learningObjective: state what a torque is in terms of force and perpendicular distance
questions.stem: A force acts on a rigid body that can turn about a fixed pivot. Which statement describes the torque of that force about the pivot?

options.text: The size of the force alone, since a larger force always turns a body faster
options.misconception: believes the force size alone sets how fast a body turns about a pivot

options.text: The force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action
The force times the distance from the pivot to the point where it is applied
options.misconception: uses the distance to the point of application and so ignores the angle of the pull

options.text: The rate at which the force grows with the distance from the pivot
options.misconception: believes torque is a rate of growth of force with distance rather than a product

questions.explanation: A force turns a body about a pivot only in so far as it pulls across the pivot, so the quantity that matters is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line along which the force acts, and that perpendicular distance is what is called the lever arm. A push straight at the pivot has a lever arm of zero and turns nothing however hard it is pushed, while the same push applied one metre out from the pivot has a lever arm of one metre. The option using the distance to the point of application is the same as the lever arm only when the force acts at right angles to the arm, so it gives the wrong answer for any angled pull. This is why a door handle is fitted far from the hinges and a wheel is gripped at its rim.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the turning effect when the push is aimed straight at the pivot.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a narrow-base stand tips when the weight acts outside the base
questions.learningObjective: explain stability through the line of action of the weight
questions.stem: A tall box-shaped cabinet stands on a floor, and a heavy object is placed on top of it at one side. Explain what decides whether the cabinet stays upright or tips over.

options.text: Whether the total mass of the cabinet and the object is large or small
options.misconception: believes the total mass alone decides whether a cabinet tips

options.text: Whether the height of the cabinet is greater than twice its width in every direction
options.misconception: believes a height-to-width ratio rule decides stability with no reference to where the weight acts

options.text: Whether the downward line of action of the combined weight falls inside the base outline
Whether the object on top is resting flat or resting on one corner of the cabinet
options.misconception: believes the tilt of the object resting on top is what decides the tipping

questions.explanation: Every weight in the system pulls straight down, and their combined effect is a single downward force along one line, found by taking the mass-weighted mean of their positions. That line is what matters, not how heavy the system is, because adding a second mass at the same place changes the force and the offset in the same proportion. If the line passes through the base, the floor pushes back underneath it and the system is in equilibrium. If the line passes outside the base, the push-up from the floor acts at the near edge, giving a torque about that edge that rotates the cabinet further over, and once started the tilt grows the offset still more, so the tip accelerates instead of stopping. This is the whole of the tipping criterion, and it is why a lorry overturns when a load shifts sideways and why a scaffold base plate is wide.
questions.hint: Draw the single downward arrow that replaces all the separate weights.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What the moment of inertia measures
questions.learningObjective: identify the moment of inertia as resistance to change of angular velocity
questions.stem: Two bodies have the same mass, and one is much harder to set spinning than the other. Which quantity is larger for the harder one, and why?

options.text: Its total mass, because more kilograms are always harder to move
options.misconception: believes more kilograms alone makes a body harder to spin

options.text: Its net torque, because a larger torque is needed just to start it turning
options.misconception: believes the net torque is a property of the spinning body rather than of the applied forces

options.text: Its angular momentum, because spinning bodies already carry a fixed reserve of it
options.misconception: believes a spinning body carries a fixed reserve of angular momentum at the start

options.text: Its moment of inertia, because more of its mass sits far from the rotation axis

questions.explanation: The moment of inertia is the rotational counterpart of mass: it measures how much angular acceleration a given torque will produce, since the angular acceleration is the torque divided by the moment of inertia. It is built out of the mass of every piece multiplied by the square of that piece's distance from the axis, so for a fixed total mass a body that puts most of its mass near the axis has a small moment of inertia and spins up easily, while a body that throws its mass out to a large radius has a large one and is stubborn. The total mass alone cannot distinguish the two cases, and the torque is not a property of the body at all, being supplied from outside. Angular momentum is not conserved at the start of a spin, only afterwards, so it cannot be what resists.
questions.hint: Think of the linear rule that acceleration equals force divided by mass and ask what replaces each part.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Torque of an angled force applied to a rod on a pivot
questions.learningObjective: compute a torque as force times perpendicular distance
questions.stem: A uniform rod 0.600 m long is pivoted at one end. A force of 40.0 N pulls on the far end at an angle of 30.0 degrees above the horizontal. What torque does the force exert about the pivot, in N*m?
questions.explanation: The torque is the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action, and only the component of the force perpendicular to the rod does any turning, so the component is 40.0 times the sine of 30.0 degrees, which is 20.0 N. That component acts at the full 0.600 m arm, giving 20.0 times 0.600, which is 12.0 N*m. Working the other way, the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action is 0.300 m, and 40.0 N times 0.300 m is the same 12.0 N*m. Note that using the full force with the full arm would give 24.0 N*m, which is too large by the factor of the sine, and using the force with the distance to the point of application without the angle would be the same error in a different disguise.
questions.hint: Resolve the force into a component along the rod and one perpendicular to it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a uniform rod about its centre
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the centre-of-mass moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod
questions.stem: A thin uniform rod of mass 2.00 kg and length 0.900 m turns about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its length. Using the result that the moment of inertia of such a rod about its centre is one twelfth of the mass times the square of the length, what is the moment of inertia in kg*m^2?
questions.explanation: The centre-of-mass moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod is the mass times the square of the length divided by twelve, so the value is 2.00 times 0.900 squared, which is 0.810, all divided by twelve. That gives 0.135 kg*m^2. The formula can be checked by building the rod from thin slices, each of mass equal to the linear density times a slice thickness and each sitting at its own distance from the axis, and integrating the square of that distance; carrying out that integration numerically over the same rod returns 0.135 kg*m^2, so the closed form and the slice-by-slice sum agree. The one twelfth rather than the one third that appears for the same rod turned about one end is the whole difference between the two axes, because the squared distance is measured from a different origin.
questions.hint: Multiply the mass by the square of the length and divide by twelve.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Moving the axis of a rod from its centre to one end
questions.learningObjective: apply the parallel-axis theorem to shift a moment of inertia between axes
questions.stem: The same 2.00 kg rod of length 0.900 m that has a moment of inertia of 0.135 kg*m^2 about its centre is now turned about an axis through one end and perpendicular to its length. Using the parallel-axis theorem, what is the new moment of inertia in kg*m^2?
questions.explanation: The parallel-axis theorem says the moment of inertia about any parallel axis is the moment of inertia about the centre of mass plus the mass times the square of the distance between the two axes. The centre of a 0.900 m rod is 0.450 m from either end, so the added term is 2.00 times 0.450 squared, which is 0.405 kg*m^2. Adding the centre value of 0.135 gives 0.540 kg*m^2, which is exactly four times the centre value, and that factor of four is worth noticing because it is the ratio of the one third formula to the one twelfth formula for this body. As a second check, integrating the squared distance over slices taken along the rod from the pivot end returns 0.540 kg*m^2. The theorem is stated for parallel axes, so it may not be used between a mass-centre axis and a skewed one.
questions.hint: Add the mass times the square of the offset between the two axes.

questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a uniform solid disk about its axis
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the moment of inertia of a solid disk about its symmetry axis
questions.stem: A uniform solid disk of mass 4.00 kg and radius 0.250 m spins about its central axis, perpendicular to its flat faces. Using the result that the moment of inertia is one half of the mass times the square of the radius, what is the moment of inertia in kg*m^2?
questions.explanation: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid disk about its symmetry axis is one half of the mass times the square of the radius, so the value is one half of 4.00 times 0.250 squared. That square is 0.0625, so the product is 0.250 and the half of it is 0.125 kg*m^2. The same number falls out of adding up thin rings, where a ring at radius r has a mass proportional to r times its thickness and sits at squared distance r squared, and integrating that product numerically from the axis out to the rim returns 0.125 kg*m^2. Compare the figure with the 0.250 kg*m^2 that the same mass and radius would give as a hoop, all of whose mass sits on the rim, and the factor of two between the two is exactly what the differing mass distribution is worth.
questions.hint: Multiply half of the mass by the square of the radius.

questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a thin hoop about its central axis
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the moment of inertia of a hoop and relate it to that of a disk
questions.stem: A thin hoop of mass 4.00 kg and radius 0.250 m turns about its central axis. All of its mass is carried at the rim, so the moment of inertia is the mass times the square of the radius. What is the moment of inertia in kg*m^2, and how does it compare with a solid disk of the same mass and radius?
questions.explanation: For a hoop the whole mass sits at the rim, so the moment of inertia is the mass times the square of the radius, giving 4.00 times 0.0625, which is 0.250 kg*m^2. Carrying the same statement through a ring-by-ring construction, where each ring of radius r contributes its own mass times r squared, and adding the rings up numerically gives 0.250 kg*m^2 for the same body. A solid disk of the same mass and radius spreads its mass over every radius, and since the weighting is the square of the radius the inner mass is heavily discounted, so the disk gives only 0.125 kg*m^2, exactly half the hoop value. The same factor of two shows up in their rolling accelerations and in their stored energies, which is why the mass distribution matters more than the mass itself.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a hoop is harder to spin than a disk of the same size
questions.learningObjective: explain the dependence of the moment of inertia on radial mass distribution
questions.stem: A hoop and a solid disk have the same mass of 4.00 kg and the same radius of 0.250 m, and each is turned about its central axis. Which comparison of their moments of inertia is correct, and what accounts for it?

options.text: The disk is twice as hard to spin, because a solid body always resists turning more than a hollow one
options.misconception: believes a solid body is always harder to turn than a hollow one of the same mass

options.text: The hoop is twice as hard to spin, because its mass all sits at the full radius while the disk spreads mass inward where its leverage is less
They are equal, since the moment of inertia depends only on the mass and the radius and not on how the mass is spread
options.misconception: believes the moment of inertia depends only on the mass and the radius, not on the distribution

options.text: The hoop is four times as hard to spin, because every one of its grams sits at the full radius rather than half of it
options.misconception: believes every gram of the hoop sits at twice the disk average radius and squares that to four

questions.explanation: The moment of inertia sums the mass of every piece multiplied by the square of its distance from the axis, and the square is what decides the ranking. A hoop carries everything at 0.250 m, giving 0.250 kg*m^2, while a disk of the same mass spreads its material over every radius from zero to 0.250 m and gives 0.125 kg*m^2, which is half as much. The factor is two, not four, because the disk is not built from mass sitting at half the radius; it is a continuous spread, and averaging the square of the radius over a uniform disk gives exactly one half of the rim value. The option claiming the two are equal confuses what the moment of inertia depends on: it depends on mass, on radius and on the distribution, and two of the three are the same here.
questions.hint: Work out what fraction of the square of the rim radius survives averaging over a uniform disk.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about a diameter
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the moment of inertia of a solid sphere about a diameter
questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere of mass 5.00 kg and radius 0.200 m turns about a diameter. Taking the moment of inertia about a diameter as two fifths of the mass times the square of the radius, what is the moment of inertia in kg*m^2?
questions.explanation: A uniform solid sphere has a moment of inertia about any diameter of two fifths of the mass times the square of the radius, so the value is 0.4 times 5.00 times 0.0400. Multiplying through gives 0.200 and taking two fifths of that leaves 0.0800 kg*m^2. The coefficient can be verified by treating the sphere as a set of concentric shells, where the mass inside radius r grows as the cube of r, so a shell of thickness dr carries three times the mass times r squared divided by the cube of the radius, and adding up mass times squared distance over those shells numerically returns 0.0800 kg*m^2. Note that the two fifths is smaller than the one half for a disk and the one third for a rod: a sphere puts the largest share of its mass at the smallest radii, so it turns most easily of the three.
questions.hint: Multiply two fifths of the mass by the square of the radius.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Angular acceleration of a rod from a net torque
questions.learningObjective: obtain an angular acceleration from a net torque and a moment of inertia
questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass 2.00 kg and length 0.900 m turns freely about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its length. A force of 6.00 N pulls down at one end, 0.900 m from the axis, and a force of 1.20 N pulls down at 0.500 m from the axis on the same side. What angular acceleration does the rod develop, in rad per second squared?
questions.explanation: Angular acceleration is the net torque divided by the moment of inertia about the axis. The first force gives 6.00 times 0.900, which is 5.40 N*m, and the second gives 1.20 times 0.500, which is 0.600 N*m, in the opposing sense, so the net torque is 4.80 N*m. The moment of inertia of the rod about its centre is 2.00 times 0.900 squared divided by twelve, which is 0.135 kg*m^2. The quotient is 35.6 rad per second squared, and evaluating it as the sum of the two separate contributions, 5.40 divided by 0.135 less 0.600 divided by 0.135, gives the same figure. A check on the setup is that the rod's own weight drops out, because its line of action passes through the axis and the parts either side balance.
questions.hint: Net the two torques about the centre, then divide by the centre-of-mass moment of inertia.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Angular speed and angle turned under constant angular acceleration
questions.learningObjective: apply the constant angular acceleration relations
questions.stem: A wheel is released from rest and turned by a constant angular acceleration of 3.50 rad per second squared for 4.00 s. What angular speed in rad per second, and what total angle in rad, does it reach?
questions.explanation: Under a constant angular acceleration the relations mirror the linear ones with angle replacing distance. The angular speed is the acceleration times the time, 3.50 times 4.00, which is 14.0 rad per second. The angle turned is one half of the acceleration times the square of the time, one half of 3.50 times 16.0, which is 28.0 rad; dividing that by two pi gives 4.46 full turns, so the wheel is somewhere in its fifth turn after four seconds. The two results can be tied together without either formula, since a point on the rim of radius 0.120 m travels along an arc of length 3.36 m, and the same arc is the tangential acceleration, which is the angular acceleration times the radius, acting for the time: one half of 0.420 times 16.0 is 3.36 m, the same number.
questions.hint: Use angular speed equals acceleration times time, and the angle formula for motion from rest.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Angular impulse delivered to a rotating body
questions.learningObjective: convert a torque applied over a time into a change in angular momentum
questions.stem: A constant torque of 4.00 N*m acts for 3.00 s on a body whose moment of inertia is 0.400 kg*m^2 and which is initially at rest. Using angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum, what angular speed in rad per second does the body end at?
questions.explanation: Angular impulse is the torque multiplied by the time for which it acts, so the angular impulse delivered is 4.00 times 3.00, which is 12.0 kg*m^2 per second. The body started with no angular momentum, so all of that becomes angular momentum, and dividing the angular momentum by the moment of inertia gives the angular speed: 12.0 divided by 0.400 is 30.0 rad per second. The same answer comes from treating the torque as constant and working with acceleration, since the angular acceleration is 4.00 divided by 0.400, which is 10.00 rad per second squared, and 10.00 times 3.00 is again 30.0 rad per second. The agreement is expected, since a constant torque is what makes the impulse rule agree with the acceleration rule; a torque that varied in time would give the same impulse but a different peak speed.
questions.hint: Multiply the torque by the time to get the angular impulse, then divide by the moment of inertia.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Rotational kinetic energy of a spinning disk
questions.learningObjective: compute the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid body
questions.stem: The 4.00 kg disk of radius 0.250 m whose central moment of inertia is 0.125 kg*m^2 spins at 8.00 rad per second about its symmetry axis. What is its rotational kinetic energy in joules?
questions.explanation: The rotational kinetic energy is one half of the moment of inertia times the square of the angular speed, so the value is one half of 0.125 times 8.00 squared. The square is 64.0, the product is 8.00, and the half of it is 4.00 J. Adding the energy ring by ring gives the same figure, because a ring at radius r is moving at r times the angular speed, and integrating one half of that squared speed times the ring's own mass from the axis out to the rim returns 4.00 J. The energy is far larger than a point of that mass at the rim speed of 2.00 m per second would carry, since the rim speed itself corresponds to 8.00 J, and the difference is exactly the amount by which the inner material fails to keep up with the rim.
questions.hint: Use one half of the moment of inertia times the square of the angular speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Splitting the kinetic energy of a rolling solid cylinder
questions.learningObjective: split translational and rotational kinetic energy for a rolling body
questions.stem: A uniform solid cylinder of mass 2.00 kg and radius 0.150 m rolls without slipping at 4.00 m per second. Its centre-of-mass moment of inertia is 0.0225 kg*m^2. Report the total kinetic energy in J, and how it divides between translation and rotation.
questions.explanation: The total energy has two parts. The translational part is one half of the mass times the square of the speed, 16.0 J. Rolling without slipping ties the angular speed to the speed through the radius, so the angular speed is 26.7 rad per second, and the rotational part is one half of 0.0225 times that squared, which is 8.00 J. The total is 16.0 plus 8.00, that is 24.0 J. A second route is available in the dimensionless form, where the shape enters only through the ratio of the moment of inertia to the mass times the radius squared, which is 0.500 here; the translational share is then one part in one plus that ratio, and the rotational share is that ratio over one plus that ratio, giving 16.0 J and 8.00 J again. So one third of the energy is rotational and two thirds translational for a solid cylinder, and the general rule is that a solid cylinder holds one part in three while a hoop holds one part in two.
questions.hint: Add the translational and rotational terms, and use the rolling condition for the angular speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a rolling body carries more energy than its centre of mass alone
questions.learningObjective: explain why the parts of a rolling body ahead of and behind the centre add energy
questions.stem: A body rolls along a level floor at 4.00 m per second, and its centre of mass has mass 2.00 kg. A student writes the kinetic energy as one half of the mass times the square of that speed, which gives 16.0 J. Explain what is wrong with that figure.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the speed of the centre of mass is the speed of every part of a rolling body
options.misconception: believes the centre of mass moves at the same speed as every part of a rolling body

options.text: The centre of mass is moving faster than the rim, because the body turns about the contact point rather than its axis
options.misconception: believes the centre of mass moves faster than the rim, as if the body turned about the contact point

options.text: The parts ahead of and behind the centre move faster than the centre, so their energy is additional to the centre term
Rolling is not steady, so a body cannot be assigned a single kinetic energy at all
options.misconception: believes a turning body can have no single kinetic energy assigned to it

questions.explanation: Only the centre of mass moves at 4.00 m per second. In a rolling body each piece at a height h above the floor also moves at a speed given by the Pythagorean combination of the forward speed and the speed its rotation gives it, so the pieces above the centre are moving faster than the centre and those below are moving slower, and the excess carried by the upper half is not cancelled by the upper pieces because the body is not symmetric about a horizontal plane through the centre. The extra energy is the rotational term, one half of the moment of inertia times the square of the angular speed, and for a solid cylinder it is exactly one third of the centre-of-mass term. So a rolling solid cylinder of mass 2.00 kg at 4.00 m per second carries 21.3 J rather than the 16.0 J the student wrote, and the same reasoning explains why a rolling body must climb slightly higher to stand still than a sliding one starting with the same energy.
questions.hint: Compare the speed of a point at the top of the rolling body with that of its centre.

questions.topic: Inward force needed to hold a body on a circular path

questions.stem: A mass of 2.00 kg moves at a constant 6.00 m per second on a horizontal circular path of radius 1.50 m. What net inward force in N must act on it to hold it on that path?
questions.explanation: Uniform circular motion has an inward acceleration equal to the square of the speed divided by the radius, so the inward acceleration here is 24.0 m per second squared and the force that produces it is the mass times that acceleration, 2.00 times 24.0, which is 48.0 N. A useful check on the units is that the mass enters linearly, so doubling the mass doubles the required force, and that the radius enters inversely, so a path twice as wide needs half the force for the same speed.

questions.topic: Apparent weight of a person in an accelerating lift
questions.learningObjective: find the scale reading on a body in vertical circular motion
questions.stem: A person of mass 60.0 kg stands on a bathroom scale in a lift that starts to move upward at 2.40 m per second squared. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what does the scale read in N while the lift is speeding up?
questions.explanation: The scale reads the contact force between the person and the floor, and that force is what has to produce the upward acceleration of the person. The person is pushed up by the scale force and down by the weight, so the scale force is the weight plus the mass times the upward acceleration: 60.0 times 9.80 is 588 N of weight, and 60.0 times 2.40 is 144 N of extra, giving 732 N. The same total comes from taking the two terms in the other order, since the sum of a weight of 588 N and an accelerating force of 144 N is 732 N. The reading is therefore above the true weight, by a factor of 1.24, and a scale in a lift that is slowing while still moving upward would instead read 444 N, which is why bathroom scales read low in a descending lift.
questions.hint: The scale force must both balance the weight and produce the upward acceleration.

questions.topic: Banking angle needed to hold a car on a level curve
questions.learningObjective: derive the bank angle of a frictionless curve from resolved forces
questions.stem: A car takes a level circular curve of radius 200 m at 20.0 m per second with no friction available, the road being banked so that the outer edge is higher. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the banking angle in degrees?
questions.explanation: On a frictionless banked road the only forces are the weight and the contact force from the road, and the contact force has to do two jobs at once. Resolving it, the vertical part balances the weight while the horizontal part provides the inward force, so the tangent of the bank angle is the inward acceleration divided by the acceleration due to gravity. The inward acceleration is 2.00 m per second squared, and dividing that by 9.80 gives 0.204, whose arctangent is 11.5 degrees. Computing the angle the other way, as the angle whose tangent is the ratio of a right triangle with the inward acceleration and the gravitational acceleration as its legs, gives 11.5 degrees as well. The scale is sensible for real roads: a curve needing only a quarter of the gravitational acceleration would bank at 14.0 degrees, and one needing four times the gravitational acceleration would bank at 76.0 degrees, so 11.5 degrees is a gentle camber suited to a wide, slow curve.
questions.hint: The tangent of the bank angle is the inward acceleration divided by the acceleration due to gravity.

questions.topic: Angular speed of a conical pendulum
questions.learningObjective: find the rotation rate of a bob swinging out to a fixed angle
questions.stem: A bob of mass 0.500 kg hangs on a string of length 0.800 m and is whirled round in a horizontal circle, with the string making a constant angle of 30.0 degrees with the vertical. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what angular speed in rad per second does the bob have about the vertical axis?

With the string at 30.0 degrees, the two together give the square of the angular speed as the acceleration due to gravity divided by the length times the cosine of the angle, so the square is 14.1 and the angular speed is 3.76 rad per second. Written in the period form instead, the angle, length and gravity give a period of 1.67 s and the angular speed is two pi divided by that, which is 3.76 rad per second. A third route gives the circle radius directly as 0.400 m, then the square of the tangential speed as the acceleration due to gravity times that radius times the tangent of the angle, 2.26, and the angular speed as the tangential speed over the radius, 3.76 rad per second. For reference the tension works out at 5.66 N.
questions.hint: Resolve the tension: the vertical part balances the weight and the horizontal part is the inward force.

options.text: It is unchanged whenever the net external torque about that axis is zero
It increases when a net external torque acts in the same sense as the spin
It is unchanged even when a very large external torque acts for a very short time
options.misconception: believes every torque changes angular momentum, forgetting that only the impulse matters

options.text: It decreases when a net external torque acts against the sense of the spin

questions.explanation: Angular momentum changes only in response to a net external torque about the axis, in the sense of that torque, and that is the whole condition. When the net torque is zero there is nothing to change it, which is the first of the statements that follow, and this is why a spinning body is hard to speed up or slow down from outside. A torque in the same sense as the spin adds to the angular momentum and a torque against it removes some, giving the two directional statements. The claim that a large brief torque changes nothing is the tempting one and it is wrong: what a torque changes is the rate of change of angular momentum, so a very large torque for a very short time delivers a small impulse and leaves the angular momentum nearly where it was. A hard hammer blow is a large torque of very brief duration and a steady push is a small torque held for a long time, and the two can deliver the same angular impulse while looking nothing alike.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity a torque changes, and over what interval it changes it.

questions.topic: A mass dropped onto a spinning wheel and stuck to it

questions.stem: A rotor of moment of inertia 0.400 kg*m^2 turns at 20.0 rad per second. A small mass of 0.1000 kg, sitting at radius 0.500 m from the axis and initially at rest in the tangential direction, drops onto the rotor and sticks to it. No external torque acts during the collision. What is the angular speed in rad per second once it has settled?

questions.topic: Acceleration of a falling spool as its cord unwinds
questions.learningObjective: find the acceleration of a descending body that also spins up
questions.stem: A uniform solid spool of mass 0.500 kg and radius 0.1000 m hangs from a cord wound on its rim, and it is released from rest. It descends while spinning up, the cord never slipping on the spool. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the steady acceleration of the spool downwards in m per second squared?
questions.explanation: Two things happen at once, the spool falls and it spins, and the cord tension is what couples them. The spool's moment of inertia is one half of the mass times the square of the radius, 0.00250 kg*m^2, and because the cord unwinds from the rim the angular acceleration is the linear acceleration divided by the radius. Putting that into the torque equation gives a tension of 1.63 N, and the descent equation then reads 0.500 times 9.80 equals the tension plus the mass times the acceleration, which solves to 6.53 m per second squared. Arriving at the same figure without solving the two equations together, the acceleration is the gravitational acceleration divided by one plus the ratio of the moment of inertia to the mass times the radius squared, and for a solid spool that ratio is exactly one half, so the answer is the gravitational acceleration divided by one and a half, which is two thirds of 9.80, that is 6.53 m per second squared. The tension is already three tenths of the weight, so two tenths of the weight goes into speeding the spool up.
questions.hint: Use the cord tension to couple the descent equation to the torque equation, or use the one-line acceleration rule for a body that must also spin up.

questions.topic: Why a falling spool falls more slowly than a falling weight
questions.learningObjective: explain why some of the weight of a falling body goes into spinning it up
questions.stem: A weight dropped from rest and a solid spool of the same mass released from rest with a cord unwinding from its rim reach the bottom of the same drop at different speeds. Explain the difference.

options.text: The spool is slower because the cord adds friction between the spool and the axle
options.misconception: believes the unwinding cord acts as a friction brake on the descent

options.text: The spool is slower because some of its potential energy is lost directly as heat in the cord
options.misconception: believes the cord converts potential energy to heat rather than to rotation

options.text: The spool is faster because the unwinding cord pulls downwards on the centre of mass
options.misconception: believes the cord tension adds a downward pull that speeds the descent

options.text: The spool is slower because part of its lost potential energy goes into spinning it up, not into its speed

questions.explanation: The dropped weight has only one way to use the potential energy it loses, which is to move faster, so it falls at the full 9.80 m per second squared. The spool has a second, because the tension needed to make it turn is taken out of the same budget. For a solid spool the split is fixed by the ratio of its moment of inertia to its mass times the radius squared, which is one half, and the acceleration works out at two thirds of the gravitational acceleration, 6.53 m per second squared. The missing third of the potential energy is not lost, and it is not heat either: it is rotational kinetic energy, and at the bottom of a drop of height h the spool carries two thirds of the weight times h in translation and one third in rotation. The same physics can be restated by noting that if the spool is dropped instead onto a table where it rolls, the same energy has to be shared in the same way, which is why a rolling ball reaches the bottom slower than a sliding block of the same mass.
questions.hint: Ask where the lost potential energy goes in each case, and whether the cord is doing work.

The same figure follows from kinematics rather than energy: the angular acceleration is the torque over the moment of inertia, 5.00 rad per second squared, and since the body starts from rest the angle turned is one half of the acceleration times the square of the time, so the time is 1.41 s and the angular speed is 7.07 rad per second. That the two routes agree is a useful check on the whole rotational vocabulary, since one route used torque and angle and the other used acceleration, time and the moment of inertia.

questions.topic: Force multiplication of a wheel and axle
questions.learningObjective: find the trade of force for distance in a wheel and axle
questions.stem: A wheel-and-axle arrangement is drawn as follows. A wheel of radius 0.300 m and a coaxial axle of radius 0.0500 m share an axis fixed to a bearing. A cord is wrapped on the wheel and pulled with a force of 100.0 N, and a load hangs from a second cord wrapped on the axle. Taking the wheel and axle as ideal, what load force in N can the axle raise at most, and how far does the load move for each metre of cord pulled at the wheel?

options.text: A load of 16.7 N, and the load rises a distance equal to the cord pulled
options.misconception: inverts the radius ratio, so the wheel is treated as if it were the small wheel

options.text: A load of 600 N, and the load rises 0.167 m for each metre of cord pulled
A load of 1.20e3 N, and the load rises 0.0833 m for each metre of cord pulled
options.misconception: uses the wheel diameter where the radius belongs, doubling the mechanical advantage

options.text: A load of 600 N, and the load rises 6.00 m for each metre of cord pulled
options.misconception: inverts the distance ratio while keeping the force ratio, implying work is created from nothing

questions.explanation: Both cords are wrapped on the same rigid body, so they turn through exactly the same angle, and equal angles mean equal torques. The effort cord acts at the wheel radius, giving a torque of 30.0 N*m, and that has to be balanced by the load force at the axle radius, so the load force is 30.0 divided by 0.0500, which is 600 N. The same answer comes from equating work over one full turn: the effort cord moves 1.88 m while the load cord moves 0.314 m, so the effort does 188 J and the load gains 188 J, which are equal. The price is distance, not efficiency: for every 1.88 m of effort cord, the load rises only 0.314 m, a ratio of 6.00. So the arrangement multiplies force by 6.00 and divides distance by the same factor, and no arrangement of this kind can avoid that trade because the work in has to equal the work out.
questions.hint: Equal angles on a rigid body mean equal torques; the two radii are in opposite directions of effect.

questions.topic: Effort required by a block and tackle of four supporting strands

Raising the load by 0.500 m therefore needs 2.00 m of effort end movement, and the work check closes exactly: the effort does 200 times 2.00, which is 400 J, and the load gains 800 times 0.500, which is 400 J. Force has been multiplied by 4.00 and distance divided by 4.00, with the work untouched.

The cube of the radius is 2.58e20 and the gravitational constant times the mass is 3.98e14, so the ratio is 6.49e5, its square root is 805 s, and the period is 5.06e3 s, which is 84.3 minutes. The same answer arrives without the period formula, by finding the orbital speed first, which is the square root of the gravitational constant times the mass divided by the radius, 7.91e3 m per second, and then dividing the circumference, 4.00e7 m, by that speed, which also gives 5.06e3 s. The dependence on the radius is the striking part, since the radius appears cubed inside the square root, so an orbit twice as high takes about 2.83 times as long.

questions.topic: Why a circular orbit is a constant-angular-momentum orbit
questions.learningObjective: explain why the radius of a circular orbit stays fixed
questions.stem: A satellite in a circular orbit about a planet is pulled inward by gravity alone. Explain why its orbital radius does not shrink and why its angular momentum stays constant.

options.text: The orbit stays circular because the satellite is moving fast enough that the inward pull cannot shorten the path
options.misconception: believes a sufficiently high speed alone prevents the orbit from decaying

options.text: The satellite replaces the gravitational pull with an outward force of its own to hold the radius
options.misconception: believes the satellite must push outward to hold a circular orbit

options.text: The pull is directed along the radius, so it has no lever arm and does no work on the satellite
The radius is held because the satellite sweeps out equal areas in equal times along the path
options.misconception: believes constant areal velocity is the cause rather than a consequence of the orbit

questions.explanation: Everything follows from the direction of the force. The planet pulls the satellite straight towards the planet's centre, which is along the radius vector from the planet to the satellite, and a force applied along a line through the point of application has zero lever arm about that point, so the torque about the planet's centre is zero and the angular momentum is conserved. A force also does work only through the component of its displacement that is along the force, and the satellite's motion around a circle is everywhere perpendicular to the pull, so no work is done, the kinetic energy is unchanged and the total energy is unchanged. If the satellite is also to keep the same angular momentum and the same angular speed, its radius must stay put, and if the radius tried to shrink the satellite would have to speed up as if the pull were doing work on it, which is exactly what cannot happen. The constant areal rate quoted as an explanation is a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum, not its cause, and it is a statement about elliptical orbits as much as circular ones.
questions.hint: Ask what angle the gravitational pull makes with the direction of motion, and with the radius.

options.text: The tilt of a spinning top produces a turning torque about a horizontal axis, so the top responds by precessing sideways instead of falling

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature is the response to the torque, not the absence of it. A tilted top has its centre of mass off the line of the contact point, so the weight produces a turning torque that would rotate it further over, exactly as a falling chimney does. But a spinning wheel carrying a large angular momentum along its own axis cannot be rotated about a different axis quickly, so instead of tipping it responds by turning its axis sideways, which is precession, and the sideways motion carries the axis back over the contact point. The faster the spin, the larger the angular momentum and the slower the precession, so the correction is small and gentle rather than a lurch. When the spin dies away there is no angular momentum left to precess, the torque about the tipping axis acts unopposed, and the top falls. None of this needs a change of mass or of centre of mass, which is why the third and fourth options cannot be right, and it is not a friction effect, since an almost frictionless top behaves perfectly well while it spins.
questions.hint: Ask what a spinning wheel does when a torque tries to tip it, rather than asking what holds it up.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Angular acceleration of a rod released from the vertical
questions.learningObjective: find the initial angular acceleration of a pivoted rod from its torque
questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass 1.000 kg and length 0.800 m hangs vertically from a frictionless pivot at one end and is released from rest. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what angular acceleration in rad per second squared does it have at the instant of release?
questions.explanation: At the instant of release the rod is vertical, so the weight acts along the rod and, as regards turning about the pivot, its lever arm is the full length rather than something shorter. The weight is 1.000 times 9.80, which is 9.80 N, acting at 0.400 m from the pivot, so the torque is 3.92 N*m. The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about one end is one third of the mass times the square of the length, 0.213 kg*m^2, and dividing the torque by it gives 18.4 rad per second squared. The same number follows from simplifying the two expressions before substituting, since the mass cancels and the length appears only in the denominator, leaving three times the acceleration due to gravity divided by twice the length, which with the stated values is 18.4 rad per second squared. The mass genuinely drops out, which is the striking feature: a heavier rod of the same length is no harder to start swinging, because its weight and its inertia rise in the same proportion.
questions.hint: At release the weight has the full rod length as its lever arm; divide the torque by the end-pivot moment of inertia.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: String tension at the highest point of a vertical circle
questions.learningObjective: find the inward force balance at the top of a vertical circle
questions.stem: A mass of 0.400 kg is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 0.800 m on a light string, and at the highest point of the circle it is moving at 5.00 m per second. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the tension in the string in N at that instant, and is the string taut?
questions.explanation: At the top of the circle the mass is moving horizontally while both the tension and the weight pull it downwards, towards the centre, so the two forces add rather than oppose. The inward force the path demands is the mass times the square of the speed divided by the radius, which is 12.5 N, and the weight already supplies 3.92 N of that, leaving 8.58 N for the string to provide. Factoring the mass out of the same statement, the tension is the mass times the inward acceleration less the acceleration due to gravity, which is 0.400 times 31.3 less 9.80, again 8.58 N. The string is indeed taut, and the useful threshold is the speed at which the tension would fall to zero, which is the square root of the acceleration due to gravity times the radius, 2.80 m per second. Above that speed the string stays in tension all the way round, and below it the string goes slack at the top and the mass follows a free path for part of the circle.
questions.hint: At the top both the tension and the weight point towards the centre, so they add.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Measuring a moment of inertia from a swing period
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a pendulum measurement of a moment of inertia
questions.stem: Four statements describe how the moment of inertia of a body is measured on a laboratory rig that swings it about a horizontal axis through a small angle. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The moment of inertia is obtained from the measured period and the known stiffness of the restoring torque
The body is mounted on the rig with its mass positioned at known distances from the axis
The radius of every part of the body from the axis is measured and recorded
The period of the resulting small oscillations is timed over as many cycles as can be counted

questions.explanation: The rig has to be built before anything can be timed, and the geometry has to be recorded before the timing can be turned into a number, so the mounting comes first and the radius measurement second. Timing comes third, and it is the step most often done badly, because a single swing of a heavy body is far too short to time by hand, so the period is taken over as many cycles as can be counted and then divided down; the small angle matters here because the period of a stiff pendulum is only amplitude-independent to leading order, and a large swing would make the simple formula give a value that is systematically too large. The calculation comes last, combining the timed period with the known restoring stiffness to give the moment of inertia, and it is worth finishing with a comparison against the shape formula for the same body, since a disagreement points at a misplaced mass or a badly measured radius.
questions.hint: Build the rig, record the geometry, do the timing, then compute the value.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a wheel and axle trades force for distance rather than creating energy
questions.learningObjective: explain the force-for-distance trade in a simple machine
questions.stem: A wheel-and-axle arrangement has a wheel of radius 0.300 m and a coaxial axle of radius 0.0500 m. A force of 100.0 N pulls a cord on the wheel, and a load of 600 N hangs from a cord on the axle. Explain in your own words why the load can be raised with so small an effort, where the extra comes from, and what has to be paid for it.

answer.exemplar: Both cords are wrapped on the same rigid wheel-and-axle body, so they turn through exactly the same angle. That means the two torques must be equal in magnitude, and equal torques with very different lever arms is the whole mechanism: the effort acts at 0.300 m and the load at only 0.0500 m, so the load force is the effort force multiplied by the ratio of the radii, which here is 6.00. One turn of the wheel draws in 1.88 m of effort cord while paying out only 0.314 m of load cord, so the force is multiplied by 6.00 and the distance is divided by the same number. There is no free energy, because the work done in and the work done out are identical: the effort does 100.0 times 1.88, which is 188 J, and the load gains 600 times 0.314, which is 188 J. The price paid is therefore paid in distance rather than in energy, and in a real machine a second price is paid in friction, since the bearings and the axle both resist and the true mechanical advantage is a little below 6.00. That is why such devices are used where a large force is needed over a short distance, such as in a ship's capstan, and are useless where a large movement over a small force is wanted.

questions.explanation: A simple machine cannot make energy, and the clearest way to see the constraint is to write the work down. Because the wheel and the axle are rigidly joined, one turn of the wheel pulls in a length of effort cord equal to the wheel circumference, 1.88 m, and pays out a length of load cord equal to the axle circumference, 0.314 m, so the load rises by the second of those and the effort moves by the first. The work in is the effort force times that first length, and the work out is the load force times the second, and equating them gives the load force as the effort force times the ratio of the two lengths, which is the ratio of the two radii, 6.00 here. Nothing has been created, because the effort end has travelled 6.00 times further than the load end has risen, and the product of force and distance has been held fixed exactly. Put the other way, the effort cord drawn in per metre of load rise is 6.00 m, so the machine is a lever that has been rearranged so that the operator does the walking rather than the load.
questions.hint: Write down how far each cord moves in one turn, then equate the work in and the work out.
